Doug's Ryders

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Further information:
They’ve won a stage. They’re second in the team standings. And now, Doug Ryder, the Tour de France’s newly anointed strategic genius, is about to make like Hannibal and storm the Alps. But as the Tour takes a break before those gruesome mountain stages.
As the African sporting story of the year—of the decade?—continues to write itself in France, Doug Ryder finds himself at the foot of the Alps, looking up at those icing-frosted monsters and pondering the Smallness of Man against the unflinching Face of Nature. Or maybe he’s chilling with croissants and coffee. Or maybe he’s just taking a bunch of meetings with bean counters in suits, all of whom want a piece of the second-place team in this, the 103rd Tour de France.
You know the story by now, right? MTN-Qhubeka are the second ranked team in the hardest professional sporting contest on earth. How did it come to this? How have a bunch of Africans and their European ringers come to dominate the Tour’s storyline? How has a rookie TdF Team Principal managed to outwit so many seasoned, European ex-dopers? Is Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula on his way to Paris to baptize Ryder in a vat of Johnny Walker Blue?
So many questions.
The story is summarized, I suppose, by what Ryder and his adept team of branders are terming “The Mandela Day Stage”—in which the British journeyman Steve Cumming, with the spectral hand of Tata Madiba on his buttocks, bolted past Romain Bardet and Thibaut Pinot to win stage 14 on a hilltop sprint. It was a miraculous sporting moment, the sort of things Disney scriptwriters routinely turn into celluloid syrup.
“It was amazing, hey?” said Ryder, when we spoke by Skype on Tuesday morning. “We had an incredible stage, it’s a dream come true for sure.” But Ryder wanted to point out that the win was followed by a top-five finish by a bloodied Louis Meintjes on stage 15.
Ryder’s technique is simple but brutal, and requires absolute buy-in from the team: the race starts, and someone needs to be in the breakaway. If cyclists hope to break free from the main group, they should expect MTN-Qhubeka cyclists with them.
It’s worked. “Now we’ve moved to second in the classifications, and we’ve been the best team on the day for three times,” says Ryder. “The team is really really trying for stage wins every day. Daniel Teklehaimanot came 7th on Day 16 of the Tour de France! It was super hard. It’s not like these breakaways are easy. You’re seeing the incredible recovery time, which has great potential for the future. It’s pretty much unheard of.”
Indeed, at 27, Teklehaimanot is coming into his own as a great Grand Tour combatant, and with riders maturing later and later - Sir Bradley Wiggins won at 33, while Ryder Hesjedal surprised the cycling world by winning the Giro d’Italia at 32 - there’s no telling what the Eritrean is capable of.
But cycling, much like war, is won by generals, not by soldiers. Doug Ryder has been shelling the front of the peloton almost every day with the Belgian Serge Peuwels, Teklehaimanot, or Louis Meinjies—a relentless offense that has provided a big payoff. And Ryder has no intention of backing off.
“Our goals are still trying to win a stage next week,” Ryder told me. “The guys are in really good spirits, and feel like they can do something next week [in the mountains.] We’ll continue racing the way we’re racing, and getting in the breakaways. We’re present and we’re up there. We can be lucky, like we have been, we need to up the road and we need to be visible.”
Like most Tours, this has been a war of attrition. Meinjies is battered from that crash on stage 15. But nor has he backed off. While most teams have lost riders, MTN remains fully staffed at nine. In wanted to know how Ryder had pulled off this miracle.
“You’ve gotta be lucky,” he said, “and it’s not like we haven’t had riders crash. But I think it goes down to the preparation of the team. We’ve had 90 percent of our guys finish in the top ten. It just shows that everybody has had an opportunity to perform and to be successful. And so all the riders are really well prepared. If you look at the Tour of Spain last year, we are one of the five teams that finished with nine riders. The guys wanna complete the race. Continuing is not a decision or a discussion or even a thought process.”
Which led me to a thought: if a rookie manager is having such success, are some big names not baying to sign up?
“Ja, I mean some of the team managers, have said we’re having a dream tour. It goes down to planning and strategy—and our lofty goals have a lot of detail behind them. The vibe in the team, a lot of people seeing us laughing, we have staff from other teams looking at us, they want to come to our to team—the freedom our riders have to perform. Serge is the number one Belgian in the Tour, and the Belgian newspapers ran a headline, ‘Sorry Serge.” We forgot about you! We disregarded you. We’re sorry. Look at Steve Cumming! They have the freedom and the trust.”
Fair enough, but can we expect a blockbuster signing?
“Well,” said Ryder, “we’ll be making strategy going forward, building the depth the team. Some really interesting individuals are coming forward. We want to bolster our Classics group”—Classics being the monster one-day European Spring races—“and to strengthen that aspect of the team.”
The team’s reputation was actually made by winning the Milan-San Remo Classic in 2013, with the German Gerard Ciolek making a break in the final moments of a weather-pocked event. Should we expect a superstar like, um, Alberto Contador to come on board?
“Look, there are a lot of good riders on the market that could join us and not change the culture,” said Ryder. “There are some amazing people who want to join this team, which is amazing for our African riders—which is ultimately what this team is about.”
The team’s budget, according to Ryder, is “between seven and ten million euro,” as compared to about 34 million euro for Sky, who currently have Chris Froome in yellow. But regardless of how much things cost, Froome has come under massive doping scrutiny, as had Team Sky. I wanted to know if Ryder thought the doping allegations had any credence.
“There’s lots of talk about Sky,” he said. “I know lots of those guys well. If you see how hard the team works, and in terms of the funding, and how they prepare. We’ve seen how you can prepare for something specifically. It just shows what preparation can do. And that’s what they do, they really do well. They really knuckled down, and it absolutely shows. We aspire to that and look up to that. Preparation and planning—you make your own luck. And I think that’s what they do.”
In the next five days, in the lead-up to Paris, legends will be made, and other legends will be secured. Many things must fall, but not excellence. Ryder will end up winning, one day. But it doesn’t matter.

Press Release:


Team MTN Qhubeka – Tour de France
It’s been called the African sports story of the year. They earned the respect of the world’s biking professionals, riding over 3000 kilometres from Utrecht to the Alps in the greatest race on earth – the Tour de France. But far from the crowds and glory there is another side to Africa’s first team at the Tour – the drive to get poor kids onto bicycles. Carte Blanche joins the team in Paris for the final stage of the Tour and later share in drinks and celebratory boerewors as we find out how they exceeded all expectations, coming fifth overall.


Script:


DOUG’S RYDERS FINAL SCRIPT TX SUNDAY 2nd AUGUST 2015

Commentary One
Eighteen months ago Doug Ryder –principle of Team MTN-Qhubeka told me he would have the first African team at the Tour De France this year. Frankly I was skeptical. So were the bosses at the Tour De France

DOUG
And they looked at me like well you are 5-10 year plan because there are no Africans in cycling, they said when do you want to be here – I said in 3 years and they laughed and said not possible!

Commentary Two
Undeterred, Doug assembled his 23 riders, some high tech science, the best doctors, mechanics, and international expertise and plunged the team into European racing.

DOUG RYDER
When we launched the team in 2012 at the UCI press conference in Holland, the other teams thought that we were crazy, they thought that we would be the Jamaican bobsleigh team – rock up no bus, no infrastructure – sit on the pavement and ride a few races and never be seen again

Commentary Three
But Doug is a dreamer, (and kept at it). At times the weather decimated his African riders, then in 2013 at this race, despite the weather, they won. 2.5 years and nearly 500 race days later, the Tour De France through them a bone- a wild card entry.

Up sound
Today history being made with Daniel Teklahaimanot!

Commentary four
On the 4th July, the Eritrean time trial champ opened the Tour De France

Cheering up sound

Commentary Five
Reinardt Janse Van Rensburg has won 14 continental races in a single year, yet he had never experienced anything like it before


Reinardt Janse Van Rensburg
There were so many people it was crazy, director shouting, crowds never seen anything like that – very nervous – confused by the shouting and screaming – like going through a tunnel

Commentary Five
Three South Africans, two Eritreans, one American and 3 Europeans were selected for the nine-man team

Derek
Is it your aim Doug to make it more African?
Doug
From a riders perspective wehave a have a feeder team that is 100% African we have 60% of our riders from the African continent, can we grow that? So we could as the depth gets better and there is more quality coming through but our international riders add a huge amount of value to this team. We will never be 100% African because of the mentorship program

Derek
And has that worked
Doug
It’s absolutely worked.

Commentary six
Three weeks, over 3000 kilometres, six hours average in the saddle. The Tour De France delivered breathtaking scenery across 3 European countries. Riders battled it out over two time trials, 9 flat, 3 hill and 7 mountain stages, ending with a grueling battle in the Alps. Louis Meintjies spent ten days training there

Louis Meintjies
Its just the next level – doesn’t compare to any races I have done before – amount of stress – tension – it is a real different feeling – you can feel it’s the biggest race in the world

Up sound TDF
As the weather started to turn the SA crashed remounted and continued to chase..




Commentary seven
By the end of the tour they would have climbed the equivalent of nearly 7 Mount Everest’s and the 22 teams would have consumed over 23 million calories.

DEREK LINK
It really is about blood sweat and tears many hopes and dreams are left shattered on the road – crashes are part of the Tour De France

Up sound
Oh there has been a massive pile up right in the centre of the field!

Commentary eight
This year the big ones came early on.

Up sound
Hooter! And a big crash has gone down there ….faded

Merhawi Kudus
Today it was very nervous, massive crash, I have never seen in my life like this crash

Reinardt Janse Van Rensburg
Ya it was quite scary we were doing 70kms – I was very lucky I crashed onto the grass nothing serious – Tyler and Daniel also came down they look a bit worse than me but its just wounds. We live to fight another day!

Commentary nine
The doctors here do a lot more than patching roasties – Dr Carol Austin
oversees five doctors including 2 with PHD’s

Carol
Ten years ago I dreamed of taking a team to the TDF – been a lot of work and I feel it’s a huge privilege to have a dream and see it realized – African talent performing at that level

Commentary ten
Carol focus is improving performance through science. She compiled these graphs to give us an idea how much output is needed for the Tour. The blue bar is energy expenditure at the Argus, versus energy expenditure in yellow at the Tour, 25 bananas versus 650 bananas; in this, the blue shows the ascents at the Argus versus the ascents in yellow at the Tour.

Up sound
First of the king of the mountains climbs and its Teklahaimanot that picks up the points

Commentary eleven
Daniel Teklahaimanot has sacrificed his family life and lived in basements across Europe, were Eritreans are often viewed as illegal immigrants. He forfeited 26 races because of visa problems

Derek
I think you said cycling is suffering
Daniel
Ja, it is suffering. For everyone it’s the same, I think we really suffer. Cycling is the hardest one of the sports, ja.

Commentary Twelve
But the suffering was about to pay off. Stage six headed to Normandy, along the coast. Apart from the cross winds, it included three testing climbs.

Phil Leggit
They have realized what is happening, its one point and we have our first African king of the mountains of the TDF
Phil legit
Sometimes dreams do come true in the Tour De France!

Commentary thirteen
For four days Daniel kept the title and if you wanted to find Daniel and his young Eritrean compatriot Merhawi, you just looked for the Eritrean flags.

DEREK LINK
But there is another side to Team MTN Qhubeka away from the cameras and the crowds and that is putting kids on bikes back home

Commentary fourteen
Founder of Qhubeka charity, businessman Anthony Fitzhenry recognized that bicycles were a low cost solution that could immediately help rural kids improve their grades

Anthony
Last year we did about 10 000 bikes and grades improved by about 50% and attendance improved by 20%

Commentary Fifteen
Anthony and Doug teamed up in 2008, and this year team MTN- Qhubeka have committed to raise funds for 5000 bicycles through the bicycles change lives campaign

Derek
What have you done differently?
Doug
When you look at our riders they have no pressure. We are like guys, we know you want to win and if you win you can benefit so many other people, and that is the motivation and the unique differentiator

Commentary sixteen
The 18th July was a hot day. Stage fourteen’s 178 kilometers included three significant climbs in the last 50 kilometers.

Phil Legitt
Steve Cummings is amongst them from MTNQ on the day that the team celebrates the birthday of the late Nelson Mandela

Commentary Seventeen
Steve Cummings has ridden for Sky, and spent the majority of his career in support of a designated team leader.

Up sound Phil Legitt
Steve Cummings - incredible result …and Steve Cummings has won the day…what an unbelievable fairy tale!

Steve Cummings
Sometimes people see the bike rider, but you have to have an unbelievable team behind you. It’s a great day especially on Mandela day

Commentary eighteen
By stage 17 – the Teams accomplishments were being written about internationally.

Up sound
Serge Pauwels from MTN Qhubeka – leaning across the top of the climb



Commentary nineteen
Out of 22 teams, MTN- Qhubeka was in second position and riders consistently made it to the top ten. It was time to eat my beret and get to Paris

Derek LINK
Really didn’t know Carte Blanche was so popular in France. Amazing they have turned out like this for us

Commentary twenty
And the respected Sir Dave Brailsford, team principal for Sky, was eating his hat too

DOUG
Dave Brailsford who runs team Sky comes to us and says jeez Doug what a dream tour, we honestly didn’t take you seriously in 2012, we all looked at you like you were smoking some cheap herb and now you are one of the most respected teams in world cycling

Commentary twenty-one
But three grueling stages in the Alps lay ahead – with the penultimate stage on Alpe D’Huez (dooez)– notorious for cracking even the world’s best riders

Up sound
And this is a superb acceleration here.. Now its hurting the Sky team

By now illness had claimed mountain climber Louis Meintjies and with only eight riders, their second team position slipped to 5th,as all the teams toiled up astonishingly steep climbs

Dr Carol Austin
This isn’t the end of the story I do believe that we will see an African athlete from our team – standing on the podium- that is stage two, the next epic book that we are going to write

Commentary Twenty-two
This year the mighty team sky led by Chris Froome was victorious, but Doug’s Ryders already have that yellow jersey in their sights.

Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 31 August 2015 Press Release: Team MTN Qhubeka – Tour de France It’s been called the African sports story of the year. They earned the respect of the world’s biking professionals, riding over 3000 kilometres from Utrecht to the Alps in the greatest race on earth – the Tour de France. But far from the crowds and glory there is another side to Africa’s first team at the Tour – the drive to get poor kids onto bicycles. Carte Blanche joins the team in Paris for the final stage of the Tour and later share in drinks and celebratory boerewors as we find out how they exceeded all expectations, coming fifth overall. Script: DOUG’S RYDERS FINAL SCRIPT TX SUNDAY 2nd AUGUST 2015 Commentary One Eighteen months ago Doug Ryder –principle of Team MTN-Qhubeka told me he would have the first African team at the Tour De France this year. Frankly I was skeptical. So were the bosses at the Tour De France DOUG And they looked at me like well you are 5-10 year plan because there are no Africans in cycling, they said when do you want to be here – I said in 3 years and they laughed and said not possible! Commentary Two Undeterred, Doug assembled his 23 riders, some high tech science, the best doctors, mechanics, and international expertise and plunged the team into European racing. DOUG RYDER When we launched the team in 2012 at the UCI press conference in Holland, the other teams thought that we were crazy, they thought that we would be the Jamaican bobsleigh team – rock up no bus, no infrastructure – sit on the pavement and ride a few races and never be seen again Commentary Three But Doug is a dreamer, (and kept at it). At times the weather decimated his African riders, then in 2013 at this race, despite the weather, they won. 2.5 years and nearly 500 race days later, the Tour De France through them a bone- a wild card entry. Up sound Today history being made with Daniel Teklahaimanot! Commentary four On the 4th July, the Eritrean time trial champ opened the Tour De France Cheering up sound Commentary Five Reinardt Janse Van Rensburg has won 14 continental races in a single year, yet he had never experienced anything like it before Reinardt Janse Van Rensburg There were so many people it was crazy, director shouting, crowds never seen anything like that – very nervous – confused by the shouting and screaming – like going through a tunnel Commentary Five Three South Africans, two Eritreans, one American and 3 Europeans were selected for the nine-man team Derek Is it your aim Doug to make it more African? Doug From a riders perspective wehave a have a feeder team that is 100% African we have 60% of our riders from the African continent, can we grow that? So we could as the depth gets better and there is more quality coming through but our international riders add a huge amount of value to this team. We will never be 100% African because of the mentorship program Derek And has that worked Doug It’s absolutely worked. Commentary six Three weeks, over 3000 kilometres, six hours average in the saddle. The Tour De France delivered breathtaking scenery across 3 European countries. Riders battled it out over two time trials, 9 flat, 3 hill and 7 mountain stages, ending with a grueling battle in the Alps. Louis Meintjies spent ten days training there Louis Meintjies Its just the next level – doesn’t compare to any races I have done before – amount of stress – tension – it is a real different feeling – you can feel it’s the biggest race in the world Up sound TDF As the weather started to turn the SA crashed remounted and continued to chase.. Commentary seven By the end of the tour they would have climbed the equivalent of nearly 7 Mount Everest’s and the 22 teams would have consumed over 23 million calories. DEREK LINK It really is about blood sweat and tears many hopes and dreams are left shattered on the road – crashes are part of the Tour De France Up sound Oh there has been a massive pile up right in the centre of the field! Commentary eight This year the big ones came early on. Up sound Hooter! And a big crash has gone down there ….faded Merhawi Kudus Today it was very nervous, massive crash, I have never seen in my life like this crash Reinardt Janse Van Rensburg Ya it was quite scary we were doing 70kms – I was very lucky I crashed onto the grass nothing serious – Tyler and Daniel also came down they look a bit worse than me but its just wounds. We live to fight another day! Commentary nine The doctors here do a lot more than patching roasties – Dr Carol Austin oversees five doctors including 2 with PHD’s Carol Ten years ago I dreamed of taking a team to the TDF – been a lot of work and I feel it’s a huge privilege to have a dream and see it realized – African talent performing at that level Commentary ten Carol focus is improving performance through science. She compiled these graphs to give us an idea how much output is needed for the Tour. The blue bar is energy expenditure at the Argus, versus energy expenditure in yellow at the Tour, 25 bananas versus 650 bananas; in this, the blue shows the ascents at the Argus versus the ascents in yellow at the Tour. Up sound First of the king of the mountains climbs and its Teklahaimanot that picks up the points Commentary eleven Daniel Teklahaimanot has sacrificed his family life and lived in basements across Europe, were Eritreans are often viewed as illegal immigrants. He forfeited 26 races because of visa problems Derek I think you said cycling is suffering Daniel Ja, it is suffering. For everyone it’s the same, I think we really suffer. Cycling is the hardest one of the sports, ja. Commentary Twelve But the suffering was about to pay off. Stage six headed to Normandy, along the coast. Apart from the cross winds, it included three testing climbs. Phil Leggit They have realized what is happening, its one point and we have our first African king of the mountains of the TDF Phil legit Sometimes dreams do come true in the Tour De France! Commentary thirteen For four days Daniel kept the title and if you wanted to find Daniel and his young Eritrean compatriot Merhawi, you just looked for the Eritrean flags. DEREK LINK But there is another side to Team MTN Qhubeka away from the cameras and the crowds and that is putting kids on bikes back home Commentary fourteen Founder of Qhubeka charity, businessman Anthony Fitzhenry recognized that bicycles were a low cost solution that could immediately help rural kids improve their grades Anthony Last year we did about 10 000 bikes and grades improved by about 50% and attendance improved by 20% Commentary Fifteen Anthony and Doug teamed up in 2008, and this year team MTN- Qhubeka have committed to raise funds for 5000 bicycles through the bicycles change lives campaign Derek What have you done differently? Doug When you look at our riders they have no pressure. We are like guys, we know you want to win and if you win you can benefit so many other people, and that is the motivation and the unique differentiator Commentary sixteen The 18th July was a hot day. Stage fourteen’s 178 kilometers included three significant climbs in the last 50 kilometers. Phil Legitt Steve Cummings is amongst them from MTNQ on the day that the team celebrates the birthday of the late Nelson Mandela Commentary Seventeen Steve Cummings has ridden for Sky, and spent the majority of his career in support of a designated team leader. Up sound Phil Legitt Steve Cummings - incredible result …and Steve Cummings has won the day…what an unbelievable fairy tale! Steve Cummings Sometimes people see the bike rider, but you have to have an unbelievable team behind you. It’s a great day especially on Mandela day Commentary eighteen By stage 17 – the Teams accomplishments were being written about internationally. Up sound Serge Pauwels from MTN Qhubeka – leaning across the top of the climb Commentary nineteen Out of 22 teams, MTN- Qhubeka was in second position and riders consistently made it to the top ten. It was time to eat my beret and get to Paris Derek LINK Really didn’t know Carte Blanche was so popular in France. Amazing they have turned out like this for us Commentary twenty And the respected Sir Dave Brailsford, team principal for Sky, was eating his hat too DOUG Dave Brailsford who runs team Sky comes to us and says jeez Doug what a dream tour, we honestly didn’t take you seriously in 2012, we all looked at you like you were smoking some cheap herb and now you are one of the most respected teams in world cycling Commentary twenty-one But three grueling stages in the Alps lay ahead – with the penultimate stage on Alpe D’Huez (dooez)– notorious for cracking even the world’s best riders Up sound And this is a superb acceleration here.. Now its hurting the Sky team By now illness had claimed mountain climber Louis Meintjies and with only eight riders, their second team position slipped to 5th,as all the teams toiled up astonishingly steep climbs Dr Carol Austin This isn’t the end of the story I do believe that we will see an African athlete from our team – standing on the podium- that is stage two, the next epic book that we are going to write Commentary Twenty-two This year the mighty team sky led by Chris Froome was victorious, but Doug’s Ryders already have that yellow jersey in their sights. metadata.Further information: They’ve won a stage. They’re second in the team standings. And now, Doug Ryder, the Tour de France’s newly anointed strategic genius, is about to make like Hannibal and storm the Alps. But as the Tour takes a break before those gruesome mountain stages. As the African sporting story of the year—of the decade?—continues to write itself in France, Doug Ryder finds himself at the foot of the Alps, looking up at those icing-frosted monsters and pondering the Smallness of Man against the unflinching Face of Nature. Or maybe he’s chilling with croissants and coffee. Or maybe he’s just taking a bunch of meetings with bean counters in suits, all of whom want a piece of the second-place team in this, the 103rd Tour de France. You know the story by now, right? MTN-Qhubeka are the second ranked team in the hardest professional sporting contest on earth. How did it come to this? How have a bunch of Africans and their European ringers come to dominate the Tour’s storyline? How has a rookie TdF Team Principal managed to outwit so many seasoned, European ex-dopers? Is Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula on his way to Paris to baptize Ryder in a vat of Johnny Walker Blue? So many questions. The story is summarized, I suppose, by what Ryder and his adept team of branders are terming “The Mandela Day Stage”—in which the British journeyman Steve Cumming, with the spectral hand of Tata Madiba on his buttocks, bolted past Romain Bardet and Thibaut Pinot to win stage 14 on a hilltop sprint. It was a miraculous sporting moment, the sort of things Disney scriptwriters routinely turn into celluloid syrup. “It was amazing, hey?” said Ryder, when we spoke by Skype on Tuesday morning. “We had an incredible stage, it’s a dream come true for sure.” But Ryder wanted to point out that the win was followed by a top-five finish by a bloodied Louis Meintjes on stage 15. Ryder’s technique is simple but brutal, and requires absolute buy-in from the team: the race starts, and someone needs to be in the breakaway. If cyclists hope to break free from the main group, they should expect MTN-Qhubeka cyclists with them. It’s worked. “Now we’ve moved to second in the classifications, and we’ve been the best team on the day for three times,” says Ryder. “The team is really really trying for stage wins every day. Daniel Teklehaimanot came 7th on Day 16 of the Tour de France! It was super hard. It’s not like these breakaways are easy. You’re seeing the incredible recovery time, which has great potential for the future. It’s pretty much unheard of.” Indeed, at 27, Teklehaimanot is coming into his own as a great Grand Tour combatant, and with riders maturing later and later - Sir Bradley Wiggins won at 33, while Ryder Hesjedal surprised the cycling world by winning the Giro d’Italia at 32 - there’s no telling what the Eritrean is capable of. But cycling, much like war, is won by generals, not by soldiers. Doug Ryder has been shelling the front of the peloton almost every day with the Belgian Serge Peuwels, Teklehaimanot, or Louis Meinjies—a relentless offense that has provided a big payoff. And Ryder has no intention of backing off. “Our goals are still trying to win a stage next week,” Ryder told me. “The guys are in really good spirits, and feel like they can do something next week [in the mountains.] We’ll continue racing the way we’re racing, and getting in the breakaways. We’re present and we’re up there. We can be lucky, like we have been, we need to up the road and we need to be visible.” Like most Tours, this has been a war of attrition. Meinjies is battered from that crash on stage 15. But nor has he backed off. While most teams have lost riders, MTN remains fully staffed at nine. In wanted to know how Ryder had pulled off this miracle. “You’ve gotta be lucky,” he said, “and it’s not like we haven’t had riders crash. But I think it goes down to the preparation of the team. We’ve had 90 percent of our guys finish in the top ten. It just shows that everybody has had an opportunity to perform and to be successful. And so all the riders are really well prepared. If you look at the Tour of Spain last year, we are one of the five teams that finished with nine riders. The guys wanna complete the race. Continuing is not a decision or a discussion or even a thought process.” Which led me to a thought: if a rookie manager is having such success, are some big names not baying to sign up? “Ja, I mean some of the team managers, have said we’re having a dream tour. It goes down to planning and strategy—and our lofty goals have a lot of detail behind them. The vibe in the team, a lot of people seeing us laughing, we have staff from other teams looking at us, they want to come to our to team—the freedom our riders have to perform. Serge is the number one Belgian in the Tour, and the Belgian newspapers ran a headline, ‘Sorry Serge.” We forgot about you! We disregarded you. We’re sorry. Look at Steve Cumming! They have the freedom and the trust.” Fair enough, but can we expect a blockbuster signing? “Well,” said Ryder, “we’ll be making strategy going forward, building the depth the team. Some really interesting individuals are coming forward. We want to bolster our Classics group”—Classics being the monster one-day European Spring races—“and to strengthen that aspect of the team.” The team’s reputation was actually made by winning the Milan-San Remo Classic in 2013, with the German Gerard Ciolek making a break in the final moments of a weather-pocked event. Should we expect a superstar like, um, Alberto Contador to come on board? “Look, there are a lot of good riders on the market that could join us and not change the culture,” said Ryder. “There are some amazing people who want to join this team, which is amazing for our African riders—which is ultimately what this team is about.” The team’s budget, according to Ryder, is “between seven and ten million euro,” as compared to about 34 million euro for Sky, who currently have Chris Froome in yellow. But regardless of how much things cost, Froome has come under massive doping scrutiny, as had Team Sky. I wanted to know if Ryder thought the doping allegations had any credence. “There’s lots of talk about Sky,” he said. “I know lots of those guys well. If you see how hard the team works, and in terms of the funding, and how they prepare. We’ve seen how you can prepare for something specifically. It just shows what preparation can do. And that’s what they do, they really do well. They really knuckled down, and it absolutely shows. We aspire to that and look up to that. Preparation and planning—you make your own luck. And I think that’s what they do.” In the next five days, in the lead-up to Paris, legends will be made, and other legends will be secured. Many things must fall, but not excellence. Ryder will end up winning, one day. But it doesn’t matter.
